Section 1
The digital arena of Twitter has become the unexpected battleground for a high-profile dispute, drawing in the Health Secretary, Jeremy Hunt, and popular comedy actor Ralf Little. What began as a seemingly routine political interview has ignited a fervent exchange over the current state of NHS mental healthcare. The controversy first surfaced when Hunt, speaking on "The Andrew Marr Show," proclaimed that the National Health Service had orchestrated "the biggest expansion of mental health provision in Europe." This assertion, intended to highlight progress, instead served as the spark for a public confrontation.

Section 2
Ralf Little, a familiar face to many from his iconic role as Anthony in the beloved sitcom "The Royle Family," wasted no time in challenging Hunt's statement. In a direct tweet, Little accused the Health Secretary of "knowingly lying" to the public, specifically targeting the statistics presented. He didn't stop there, issuing a bold challenge: if Hunt believed his claims were accurate, Little encouraged him to take legal action and sue him. This direct and combative response immediately amplified the unfolding Twitter spat.

Section 3
This was not the first time Hunt's figures regarding mental health staffing had come under scrutiny. Just a month prior, he had apparently overstated an increase in mental health workers, claiming 30,000 when the actual figure was significantly lower, reportedly only 43 times the real number. Undeterred by the past correction, Hunt responded to Little a week after the initial tweet. He launched a counter-offensive, a series of statistics aimed at bolstering his original statement, and a "double dare" for Little to disprove his new evidence.

Section 4
Little, proving to be a formidable opponent in this digital debate, did not back down. He responded with an extensive thread of over 40 tweets, meticulously dissecting and rebutting Hunt's claims. His arguments were bolstered by statistics sourced from an independent UK fact-checking charity, Full Fact, lending significant credibility to his side. This detailed rebuttal resonated widely, with the thread going viral and being shared more than 15,000 times, demonstrating public interest and engagement.

Section 5
The argument, having gained considerable momentum, has continued to unfold on Twitter. On Monday, Hunt fired back with his own lengthy response, a series of 26 tweets. While the sheer volume of tweets aimed to address Little's points, the chronology within Hunt's thread became muddled, rendering it somewhat difficult to follow. Hunt directly addressed Little's accusation of lying, questioning his ability to substantiate such a "strong claim." He presented further data, including figures on nurses in training and an overall increase in nurse training places, and even cited a New York Times article, though this particular article had a history of being corrected after challenges from former shadow minister for mental health, Luciana Berger. The debate, it seems, is far from over.
